Worth reading: OpenAI new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint. Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will come with a local compact: paying the full cost of its energy and grid connection, publishing water and electricity use, hiring locally, and investing in priorities chosen by residents.
 https://lnkd.in/eQTmUf-y

Yes, the midterm result plays a part. Still, it sets a reference for what it means to turn AI infrastructure, and any infrastructure, into a driver of local development and social impact. We can debate whether this is the right approach, or enough. Is this the AI Social Contract? NO, but it is a starting point.

It also says something about corporate accountability. OpenAI itself asks policymakers to set clear rules, because voluntary commitments are not enough. Rules do not stop investment. They make sharing the value a design specification rather than an afterthought.

This is business changing direction to work for society. It is what we work on every day at PlusValue (PV): aligning private and public interests by redesigning the infrastructure investment policy so that social outcomes are built in from the start.

💔 This is a difficult post to write, but it’s important to be honest about where I’m at right now. A little while ago, I accepted what I believed was a stable, full-time opportunity. After conversations, negotiations, and assurances about the future, I was encouraged to put my own creative work with Napkin Studios aside and focus entirely on the company.

And I did. Because I trusted the people I was working with. I believed in what we discussed and thought I was stepping into something long-term.

Unfortunately, that opportunity was taken away almost as quickly as it came, without warning or time to prepare because of budget constraints.

It’s frustrating. Not just because I lost a job, but because I made decisions about my livelihood based on promises I believed in. When something like that changes overnight, there’s no magical reset button. You still have bills, responsibilities, and a life to maintain.

I am, asking my network for a little help.

I’m looking for work immediately. Full-time would be ideal, but I’m open to contract opportunities as well.

I have 14+ years of experience across product design, mobile/web design, visual design, branding, creative direction, and everything in between. I’ve been fortunate to work on projects for companies like Google and Disney, alongside startups and growing businesses.

I’m not looking for a handout. I’m looking for an opportunity to do what I love, contribute something meaningful, and have a little stability again.

I also want to acknowledge something that’s been weighing on me.

Being a creative right now is hard. With AI transforming our industry at such an incredible pace, navigating an already competitive job market has become even more complicated. We’re expected to constantly adapt, evolve, and prove our value in ways that can honestly feel exhausting.

I know I’m not alone.

I see so many incredibly talented designers, artists, and creatives sharing similar stories. People with years of experience who just want to work, create, and support themselves.

I’m not complaining. I’m not asking for special treatment. I just want a fair opportunity and a little room to breathe.

I’m sharing this because I know how isolating this experience can feel, and because sometimes asking for help is the hardest part.

If you know of anyone hiring, have a referral, need an experienced designer, or could simply share this post with your network, I’d appreciate it more than you know.

You can see my work here:
https://napkin-studios.com 

I also have private case studies available upon request because of NDA.

To all my fellow creatives navigating layoffs, uncertainty, rejection emails, or just trying to figure out what’s next, please hang in there

I genuinely hope nobody has to experience this kind of situation. If you’re going through something similar, I’m rooting for you too. If you need someone to talk to do not hesitate to reach out. ❤️

Thank you for taking a moment to read this. It really means a lot.

Your development contract is quietly absorbing risk you never agreed to take on.

• Fixed price works only when scope is truly final — every change triggers a renegotiation and gives vendors a chance to recoup margin they priced in defensively
• T&M is the honest model for uncertain scope, but breaks down without strong product management and transparent reporting on your side
• A dedicated team bills at a flat monthly rate per person and builds context over time — codebase knowledge, past decisions, technical debt — which resets to zero every time you switch vendors
• Most product companies eventually move to a dedicated model because fixed price and T&M both reset context and renegotiate scope with each engagement
• The right question is not about rates — it is about who absorbs the risk when scope shifts and how much management overhead lands on you

Imagine hiring a logistics partner to move goods across the country—and agreeing to pay them for every hour their trucks sit idling in traffic, regardless of whether a single package reaches the customer.

Nobody would sign that contract for their supply chain. Yet for decades, enterprises signed that exact deal for their front office.

While back-office transformation re-engineered ERPs and supply chains around strict unit economics, marketing, sales, and customer experience remained trapped in an effort-based retainer model—paying for agency hours, FTE headcount, and campaign volume rather than revenue impact.
Front-Office Transformation means trading the "hourly truck rental" for an Outcome-Based Marketing-as-a-Service (MaaS) model—an integrated growth engine paid on delivered business milestones:
🎯 Brand Awareness (Paying for Market Entry, Not Billboards): Instead of measuring creative asset volume, you scale high-velocity, brand-safe storytelling tied to qualified reach, share of voice, and branded search lift. 
🚀 Customer Acquisition (Paying for Qualified Pipeline, Not Foot Traffic): Unifying first-party signals across marketing and sales to target high-intent buyers—anchoring commercials to lower Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) and pipeline velocity.
📈 Conversion Lift (Paying for Closed Orders, Not Storefront Visits): Replacing static, one-size-fits-all funnels with continuous AI experimentation and real-time next-best-action decisioning—measured by checkout completion and incremental revenue.
🔄 Customer Retention & LTV (Paying for Repeat Business, Not Loyalty Cards): Detecting churn signals early and orchestrating proactive lifecycle engagement—tying success to repeat purchase rates, net revenue retention, and lifetime value.

When your front-office operating model shifts from "how many hours did we bill?" to "how much incremental revenue did we deliver?", silos between marketing, sales, and service disappear—and your front office transforms from a discretionary expense into a compounding growth engine.

If you’re leading a front-office transformation right now, which outcome is your 
#1 priority: lowering CAC, lifting conversion, or driving retention?

A career break doesn't make your skills expire. Standing still does.
 
Tech changes every few months. After a break, the gap that employers worry about is rarely the time away. It is the doubt about whether your skills are current. The good news: that is the part you can fix, and faster than you think.
 
Here is a 5 step comeback plan, built around skills.
 
1. Audit before you upskill
 List what you knew, what has changed and what is in demand now. Match it to one target role. Most returners lose months learning the wrong things.
 
2. Keep what lasts, refresh what doesn't
 Problem solving, system thinking, debugging and stakeholder communication stay with you. Tools, frameworks and cloud platforms need a refresh. Start there.
 
3. Learn in public, in small steps
 30 to 60 minutes a day beats a weekend binge. Pick one core skill each month (cloud, data, DevOps, QA automation or AI-assisted work) and finish one small project with it.
 
4. Turn learning into proof
 Publish it. A GitHub project, a short write-up or a certification tells a recruiter more than 'currently upskilling' ever will. Add it to your profile and mention it in your first message to a recruiter.
 
5. Stay current by habit, not by panic
 Follow two or three trusted sources, join one community and review job descriptions for your role every month. The skills employers ask for are your syllabus.
 
THE STRONG TAKEAWAY
 Employers hire for recent, relevant, proven skills. A career break is a gap in dates. Skills are a gap in evidence. Close the second one and the first matters far less.
 
AND FOR EMPLOYERS
 The strongest returners are often the most motivated learners in the room. Great employers support them with:
 - Skills-based hiring, not gap-based screening
 - A structured onboarding or returnship
 - A mentor in the first few months
 - Time to refresh skills on the job
 - A clear path from contract or contract-to-hire to a permanent role

My churn model scored 74% accuracy. A model that always predicts 'no churn' scores 73.5%.
That is why I stopped trusting accuracy and built ChurnGuard around recall.ChurnGuard is an end-to-end ML project that predicts which telecom customers are likely to leave, so a retention team knows who to contact first.

What is inside:
• XGBoost model tuned for recall: 79% recall and 0.84 ROC AUC on a held-out test set (IBM Telco dataset, 7,043 customers)
• SHAP explanations: contract type, tenure, and monthly charges drive the risk
• FastAPI service with API-key authentication and Pydantic input validation
• Docker and GitHub Actions CI/CD: automated tests, container health checks, and image publishing
• Deployed on Azure Container Apps
The video shows the repository architecture, a live authenticated prediction (200 OK) via Swagger UI, and the passing GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline.

What I learned:
• Testing, containerization, and deployment took more effort than modelling.
• I caught a data leakage mistake (scaling before splitting) and fixed it.Known limitations are documented in the README: public dataset, static decision threshold, and not yet tested on live production traffic.

Full stack AI features live or die on the contract between the model and your code. Here is a design decision I made on a Python and React.js project that I'd make again.

The project was an expense categoriser and cashflow forecaster for SME finance. Users upload bank CSVs and the app uses an LLM to categorise each transaction.

The first version let the model return free text, then parsed it with regex. It worked on the examples I tried and broke on the first messy description.

The trade-off I chose:

→ Free text: fast to prototype, flexible, fragile in production. Every parser change is a bug risk.
→ Structured outputs: a fixed schema with allowed categories, validated before anything touches PostgreSQL. More upfront work, far fewer silent failures.

My rule now: if the output will be stored, displayed as data or used to make a decision, define the schema first. Use free text only for things a human reads and nothing downstream depends on.

For full stack engineers, this also means the React.js front end and the Python backend agree on the same types, so a model change can't quietly break the UI.

Hiring managers, I'd like to know how you decide between flexible and strict output formats on your AI features. Engineers, what has bitten you most: the model, the parser, or the schema?

The 2027 Agent Builder: A Zero-to-Shipped Roadmap That Starts With One Loop, Not One Framework
#UpSkillRealm

1. The Mental Model & The Prerequisite Foundation
An AI agent consists of four core parts: a language model, a set of tools, a loop, and a stop condition. Beginners fail because they adopt heavy frameworks before understanding the loop underneath.
 * The Six-Week Prerequisite: Skip ML theory and GPUs. Spend six weeks mastering Python basics, HTTP/JSON parsing, environment variables, and reliable API calls with proper error handling.
 * Prompts as Specifications: Treat system prompts as strict job descriptions containing four sections: role, task, constraints, and output schema.

2. Core Engineering Disciplines
 * Hand-Built Loops First: Code a message list, tool registry, dispatcher, and step cap manually. You will immediately encounter malformed arguments, repeated calls, and infinite loops—fix these with deterministic code, not prompt tweaks.
 * Tools as Contracts & MCP: Design atomic, single-job tools with three-sentence descriptions (what it does, when to use it, what it returns), capped output sizes, and actionable error messages. Wrap them in a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server—the baseline interoperability standard for 2027.
 * Three-Layer Memory: Manage working memory (context window), session memory (active scratchpad), and long-term memory (persisted facts). Summarize tool outputs aggressively so agents don't drown in history.
 * Four-Layer Evals: Build 30 test tasks with known outcomes before tuning. Grade tool selection, argument correctness, final answer, and trajectory independently to diagnose failures systematically.
 * Disciplined Multi-Agent Scaling: Only use orchestrator-worker patterns when subtasks are genuinely independent, always benchmarking against a single-agent baseline to justify token overhead.

3. The 2027 Hiring Portfolio
Hiring managers no longer screen for framework buzzwords. Ship three public projects—one hand-built loop, one MCP server, and one evaluated agent with full execution traces—accompanied by write-ups detailing what broke and how you debugged it.

India’s two largest IT firms want up to 14,900 forward deployed engineers. About 1,200 people in India are ready for the role today.
 
The plans:

 • TCS: 1–1.5% of its workforce, or 5,900 to 8,900 people (Reuters)
 • Infosys: 6,000 over the next few years
 • Ready supply: about 1,200 (CIEL HR)
 
Two other numbers say more about what happens next:

 • 75–80% of FDE job postings in India are solutions or implementation roles with a new title (Source: UnearthInsight)
 • 47% of enterprises plan to upskill their own engineers, and 31% plan to hire from outside (Source: Scaler-CMR Report)
 
So most of India’s FDEs will be today’s engineers with a course and a new designation.
 
Whether that works depends on the contract. An FDE needs permission to:

 • Sit with the people doing the work
 • Change the systems they use
 • Answer for whether it still runs next week
 
A fixed-scope services contract grants none of this. Put a newly trained FDE back inside one and the work is still implementation.
 
Employers know where the difficulty lies:

 • 51% test FDE candidates with a deployment or troubleshooting case, and 24% with a coding test
 • Production deployment: 77% call it important, 19% can find it
 • Customer engagement: 61% call it important, 25% can find it
 
Neither is mainly an AI skill. Engineers learn both by owning a system at a customer when it fails. Training can rehearse that. It can’t hand anyone the pager.
 
The squeeze lands on software companies. Close to 80% of FDE hiring is in Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Hyderabad, at ₹70–90 lakh a year for experienced people. A platform vendor hiring one FDE now bids against TCS and Infosys, and the role stays open another quarter.

At KnackLabs, forward deployed engineering has been in our DNA since 2016: our engineers sit with the customer’s team from discovery to production, and answer for what runs after launch.

One question sorts the market: when the system fails at the customer at 2 am, whose phone rings?
 
If it’s a ticket queue, the engineer was never forward deployed.

HRBP in the IT Sector: Is Your Business Scaling Faster Than Your People Systems?

Growing an IT company from 10 to 250 employees is not just about winning more projects, hiring developers and expanding technical capabilities.

At some point, the challenges that affect business growth are no longer purely technical. They become people and organisational challenges.

Consider a few situations:
1. Your project pipeline is growing, but are your skills keeping pace?
You may have developers on your payroll, yet struggle to find the right capabilities for an upcoming project. Hiring externally becomes the immediate solution, while existing employee skills and internal mobility remain underutilised.

2. Your best developers are becoming managers. But are they equipped to lead people?
Technical expertise doesn't automatically translate into people-management capability. Without structured support, managers can struggle with performance conversations, team conflicts, employee motivation and accountability.

3. You are hiring to meet demand, but what happens when project requirements change?
Are you forecasting workforce requirements against your actual project pipeline? Could better resource allocation, skills mapping and cross-training reduce unnecessary hiring and unproductive capacity?

4. Your attrition numbers look manageable, but are you losing the right people?
Losing one critical architect, project lead or experienced developer can have a disproportionate impact on delivery continuity, client relationships and team performance.
Are you measuring attrition only as a percentage, or understanding its impact on business operations?

5. You have introduced performance appraisals, but do they measure business contribution?
Are employees evaluated against meaningful delivery outcomes, quality, collaboration, innovation and role-specific expectations, or primarily through task completion and subjective manager feedback?

6. Your organisation is adopting AI, but is your workforce evolving with it?
Are job responsibilities changing? Are employees being reskilled? Are managers prepared to lead teams where human capabilities and AI-enabled productivity work together?

These are not isolated HR problems. They are business challenges with people at their centre.

What can a Strategic HR Business Partner bring to a growing IT business?

Skills-based workforce planning aligned with project demand.
Resource utilisation and internal talent deployment strategies.
Technical manager development and leadership coaching.
Performance frameworks linked to delivery and business outcomes.
Critical talent retention and career progression.
People analytics that help leadership anticipate workforce risks.
AI-related workforce transformation and change management.

The objective is not to introduce more HR processes or technology for the sake of it.
It is to help business leaders make better workforce decisions, strengthen management capability and build an organisation that can scale without creating unnecessary operational complexity.

For IT founders and CEOs leading teams of 10–250 employees:

Are your current people systems equipped for the next stage of your business growth?

I would be interested in exchanging perspectives with technology business leaders on where people strategy can make a measurable difference.

If you are exploring strategic HRBP support on a contract or part-time basis, I would welcome a conversation.

Let's make people's strategy a business advantage.
